One Lot, Multiple Possibilities: Could Your Tucson Property Be Worth More as a Development Site?

A modest home on a large lot may have possibilities that aren't obvious from the street.

By Reddy Appraisal LLCOctober 22, 20262 min read

IN THIS ARTICLE

Development potential is not approvalVerify legal, physical and financial constraintsEstablish a market-value starting pointMore in Land & Redevelopment ↗← All 24 articles

THE SHORT ANSWER

Tucson and Pima County contain very different neighborhoods and development conditions, so parcel-level research is essential. Whether you're holding a vacant residential lot or considering the future of an existing home, a well-supported land or residential appraisal can help establish a market-value starting point for your next conversation with planners, builders, and lenders.

Development potential is not approval

A modest home on a large lot may have possibilities that aren't obvious from the street. Depending on location and local rules, a property owner might explore an additional residence, a lot split, or another residential use. But development potential isn't the same as development approval—or guaranteed added value.

Verify legal, physical and financial constraints

Start by verifying zoning, minimum lot standards, setbacks, access, utility capacity, easements, and any subdivision or permitting requirements with local officials. Next, compare likely development costs and timelines with what buyers are paying for finished homes and similar land. A property's highest and best use must be supported by legal, physical, financial, and market evidence—not simply by what could look good on a site plan.
